title: Pauri 5, meaning: one Giver
hook: He cannot be installed or made; the Guru has given one understanding, that there is one Giver of all, never to be forgotten (Japji 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, niranjan, the stainless one, and the sound of pauri five. Your line was thaapiaa na jaae.

Have you ever forgotten who gave you something? A sweater you've worn for years, and one day you realize you have no idea where it came from. A habit picked up from a teacher whose name is gone. People forget givers all the time, not out of ingratitude, just because the gift becomes part of them. The fifth pauri ends with Nanak asking for one thing only: not to forget the Giver.
screen: `A SWEATER, BUT FROM WHOM?` → `THE GIFT BECOMES PART OF YOU.` → `DON'T FORGET THE GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. He cannot be installed or made; He is Himself, by Himself, the stainless one. Those who serve Him receive honor. Nanak, sing of the treasure of virtues. Sing, listen, and keep love in your heart: pain will leave, and peace will come home. Then a run of lines about the Guru's word. Through the Guru comes the sound, through the Guru the scripture, and through the Guru the One is everywhere. The Guru, it says, is Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma; the Guru is Parvati, the mother. Sikh commentators read this as saying that everything people honor in those great names is found in the Guru's word. Then Nanak says something disarmingly honest: even if I knew Him, I couldn't describe Him; there's no telling it. And then the refrain. Guraa ik dehi bujhaaee: O Guru, give me this one understanding. Sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa, so mai visar na jaaee: of all living beings there is one Giver; may I not forget Him. Visar is to forget, to let slip from the mind; na jaaee, may it not happen. That's the whole request. Not wealth, not answers to every question, not even the power to describe God. Just memory. If there is one Giver of everything, forgetting the Giver is the main thing that can go wrong. And remembering is simran, the practice from camp three, the thing Japji's title word, jap, asks for.
screen: `NOT INSTALLED, NOT MADE.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE.` · `ONE GIVER OF ALL BEINGS.` · `VISAR — TO LET SLIP.` · then, large: `MAY I NOT FORGET.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing within reach, something you're wearing or the cup you last drank from, and trace it back: who made it, grew it, carried it, paid for it, until the chain runs out into rain and soil and sun. Notice how many hands there are, and where they all begin. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver with a single word, Waheguru.
Visar. To forget, to let slip from the mind: the one thing Nanak asks never to do, of the one Giver of all beings.
Your line: may I not forget. Of all living beings, there is one Giver. Day one hundred seventy-two, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the fifth pauri each morning; its refrain, that there is one Giver of all beings who should never be forgotten, is also sung as kirtan.

original.say: SUBH-naa JEE-aa kaa IK DAA-taa, so mai VI-sar na JAA-ee
original.note: Gurmukhi: the refrain of pauris 5 and 6: one Giver of all beings; may I not forget Him.

trapdoor: what it means: of all beings there's one Giver; the one request is not to forget Him.
what a scholar hears: the line naming the Guru as Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma and Parvati is read by Sikhs as the Guru's word containing all that those names are honored for.
recall: the divine order that all forms come by
a person who has become true

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 5

notes: Pauri 5 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
'Gur eesar gur gorakh barmaa gur paarbatee maaee': gorakh is read as Vishnu by many, and by some as Gorakhnath. The script says Vishnu. Keeper should decide, and check the interpretive sentence.
The Hindu names are handled descriptively without ranking; check tone.
